newsitem.title: FRANCE: Veteran Communist Marchais to quit French assembly.
newsitem.headline: Veteran Communist Marchais to quit French assembly.

text.p: Veteran former French Communist party leader Georges Marchais, 76, announced on Monday he would not seek re-election to parliament at the next general election in 1998.

Marchais, a hardliner who retired as party leader in 1993, told the Communist daily L'Humanite: "I'll be 78 then and will have been in parliament for 25 years. It's a long time and a very demanding job."
Marchais had led France's once-powerful Communist party, long one of Moscow's staunchest allies in Western Europe, from 1972 until he handed over to his more liberal successor Robert Hue.

Even after he turned over the leadership, Marchais remained in the politburo and was widely regarded as heading an old guard of hardliners resisting Hue's efforts to modernise and liberalise the movement.
Marchais, a former metalworker who approved Soviet intervention in Afghanistan in 1979, admitted in a recent television interview that the party was slow to evolve under his rule.
"I am a Communist and will remain a Communist until I die. I believe in the need to strengthen the party and I'll keep on working on its ideas," he said.
Under Marchais, the Communists' share of the vote declined from 25 to just seven per cent as the Soviet communism that inspired him was discredited, then swept away.
The French communists were slow to reform, unlike their Italian sister-party, which ditched its extremists, adopted social democracy and changed its name after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
Hue has gradually shifted the party towards qualified acceptance of the market economy and the European Union, although it rejects a single European currency.

During last year's presidential campaign, in which he stabilised the Communist vote at 8.6 percent, Hue repudiated Marchais' line that the record of Communist rule in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe was "globally positive".
Hue is now positioning the party to be a coalition partner with the Socialists in the 1998 general election, reaching out beyond the Communists' traditional proletarian power-base.
Marchais never criticised his successor publicly but was reported to have sniped at him in politburo sessions over the party's more liberal line and rapprochement with the Socialists.
